data.title: Deutsche Bank CEO says clients calm after data leak
data.description:
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing on Thursday said clients were calm after a major leak of internal records and that Germany's largest lender was not seeing an impact on business.

The leak ​of 15 million internal records reported this week has renewed scrutiny of the German lender's past dealings ‌with clients ⁠including Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

"If you ask, what is the client reaction since Tuesday? Very calm," Sewing said at a financial conference.

"We have built trust and confidence with our clients," he added, noting that the bank was not currently seeing any impact on business.

The ordeal dealt a major setback to ​Sewing's efforts to restore the lender's reputation.

"This is a totally different bank ... Certain issues happened in the past. They have been worked on," he said.

data.title: East Timor eyes boost in business funding through instant payment system
data.description:
By Jun Yuan Yong

East Timor, one of the world's poorest countries, hopes to close a funding gap for its small businesses and help integration with the regional bloc ASEAN through a new instant payment system, its central bank governor said on Thursday.

  • East Timor needs to spur private sector economic activity, as a big proportion of its economy is driven by informal businesses unable to secure loans, Governor Hélder Lopes told Reuters

  • Through digital payments, a system for which was introduced in September, lenders can use transaction information to assess if businesses are viable for financing, Lopes added

  • Asia's youngest country formally joined the Association of Southeast Asian Nations last year after a 14-year wait to become the bloc's 11th member

  • East Timor's 2025 gross domestic product was about $1.9 billion, according to the World Bank, a fraction of ASEAN's combined GDP of more than $3.8 trillion

  • Lopes said the country was seeking to "level up" to ASEAN's standard to support financial and economic integration and digitalisation

  • "Our financial sector is highly liquid and we have a huge amount of excess liquidity but the issue is channelling this to our economic activities," he said on the sidelines of a fintech event in Singapore

  • The World Bank in a report last year said East Timor was entering a "potentially transformative" economic chapter but needs to move beyond oil and gas and improve private sector productivity

  • Lopes also said East Timor, which uses the US dollar, has benefited from the strength of the dollar against the rupiah of neighbouring Indonesia, the source of most of its imports

data.title: Copper Remains Under Pressure After Wave of Selling — Market Talk
data.description: Copper prices remain near their lowest level since April following a broad selloff across commodity markets, driven by a stronger U.S. dollar and growing concerns over AI-related investment. In early European trading, three-month copper futures on the LME fall 0.7% to $12,531.50 a metric ton, putting the metal on track for a weekly decline of 9%. "Concerns around the pace of data centre build out are weighing significantly on copper, even if not much has changed for 2027 build plans," analysts at Morgan Stanley say. The weakness comes despite constrained global mine supply and tight inventories in China. Meanwhile, expectations of higher interest rates are adding to the pressure, as elevated borrowing costs could weigh on industrial investment and strengthen the dollar, making dollar-denominated commodities more expensive for overseas buyers. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)

data.title: NetEase Profit, Revenue Fall Amid Lackluster Gaming Performance
data.description:
(08:34 GMT) *NetEase 3Q Games and Related Value-Added Services Rev CNY22.9B, Down 1.7% on Year >NTES
(08:35 GMT) *NetEase: 3Q Games Rev Falls From Lower Rev in Some Self-Developed Games >NTES
(09:09 GMT) NetEase Profit, Revenue Fall Amid Lackluster Gaming Performance

By Sherry Qin

NetEase's earnings disappointed following lackluster performance of its self-developed games in the third quarter and the absence of a major blockbuster release.

China's second-largest game company said Thursday that quarterly revenue fell 1.8% from a year earlier to 27.85 billion yuan, equivalent to $4.18 billion. That missed the 30.44 billion yuan expected of analysts polled by Visible Alpha.

Net profit declined 2.6% to 8.40 billion yuan, also lower than market expectations of 9.45 billion yuan.

Adjusted net profit, a closely watched metric that excludes share-based compensation expenses, fell 3.2% to 9.50 billion yuan.

NetEase said revenue from games and related value-added services fell 1.7% due to lower revenue from some self-developed games. That compared with 9.7% growth in the previous quarter.

The underwhelming performance comes as growth in China's game market moderates in the second half after a strong start to the year, partly because of a high base for PC games. There was also a lack of blockbuster titles during the critical summer holiday season.

For NetEase, its top line was dragged by the robust performance of evergreen game "Fantasy Westward Journey" last year and the subdued performance of recently launched "Sea of Remnants," Nomura analysts said ahead of the results.

The next highly anticipated title, "Ananta," an open-world role-playing game, is slated to be released in January.

Together with NetEase's evergreen titles, this game could help accelerate gaming revenue growth to 10% from single digits this year, HSBC analysts said in a recent note.

Write to Sherry Qin at sherry.qin@wsj.com

data.title: Anthropic IPO: Here Are 3 Critical Questions Morningstar Wants Investors To Ask
data.description:
Key points:
  • Morningstar analysts see Anthropic’s growth hinging on enterprise AI adoption, model capabilities, and revenue. 
  • Analysts see nearly $360 billion in annual revenue for Anthropic by 2031. 
  • Morningstar sees stronger AI models and research driving growth for Anthropic. 

Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) investment case boils down to three critical questions, according to Morningstar. The firm believes the AI startup’s long-term prospects depend on growing enterprise adoption, continued advances in model skills, and its ability to monetize those improvements, with revenue expected to reach nearly $360 billion by 2031.

ANT’s Enterprise Demand, AI Progress And Monetization Take Center Stage

In a report published after reviewing Anthropic's regulatory filing in November, Morningstar analysts Malik Ahmed Khan and Tucker Hawthorne identified three factors that could shape Anthropic's financial future: whether businesses will continue expanding their AI usage, whether technological improvements will create additional commercial opportunities, and whether Anthropic can turn its products into sustainable revenue.

The analysts remain positive on all three fronts and suggest Anthropic could post nearly $360 billion in annual revenue by 2031. Anthropic’s public listing is valued at $1.5 trillion at $83 a share, above the expected range.

Anthropic Enterprise AI Adoption Could Have Room To Grow

According to the analysts, some investors question whether companies will continue increasing their AI spending. While businesses have budget limits, large enterprises have the resources to develop exclusive technology or rely on less expensive alternatives.

However, Morningstar believes these concerns ignore how early businesses remain in adopting AI solutions. Anthropic is also attracting customers beyond major technology companies, reducing its dependence on those capable of developing competing products.

Better AI Models Could Unlock New Revenue Opportunities

Morningstar also sees opportunities for Anthropic to maintain its technical edge as AI development progresses.

The analysts highlighted three advantages. First, Anthropic's use of AI in its own research could boost model development, while restrictions on competitors copying its technology may help protect it against open-weight alternatives.

More advanced models could help Anthropic handle complex tasks and serve businesses willing to pay more for AI solutions. The company is also developing products for industries where demand for advanced AI is still growing.

Monetizing AI: A Challenge For Anthropic

Despite the positives, Morningstar acknowledged that Anthropic faces risks in converting its tech products into financial returns. Cheaper AI products could become capable enough for many customers, thereby limiting Anthropic's pricing power.

Anthropic: Retail View 

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ANT stock was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘extremely high’ message volumes.

A user said, “Market makers set up shorts. As soon as market opens $ANT is going to make things beserk and shoot everything up.”

data.title: TCS-Bosch Deal Could Shift Up To 3,000 Employees From Captive Technology Operations
data.description:
The exploratory discussions could give TCS access to engineering teams while helping Bosch evaluate its technology operations and cost structure

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) is in early discussions to acquire part of Bosch’s technology and product development operations in India, in a potential transaction that could involve the transfer of up to 3,000 employees, according to a report by Mint.

The proposed deal remains at an exploratory stage, with discussions expected to move to the board level next month before any decision is taken. The scope of the operations involved, the number of employees who may move and the final terms of the transaction have not been determined.

The potential acquisition comes as Bosch evaluates options to reduce costs by transferring some of its technology and product development activities. For TCS, the transaction could strengthen its engineering capabilities and provide access to specialised talent working on emerging technologies, including physical artificial intelligence (AI).

Bosch Evaluates Technology Operations

According to the Mint report, Bosch is considering the sale of a part of its India-based technology and product development operations as part of its cost-containment efforts.

The proposed transaction could give TCS access to engineering teams involved in technology development and product engineering. The opportunity comes amid growing interest in physical AI, which involves integrating artificial intelligence into machines and physical systems, including robotics and autonomous vehicles.However, the discussions remain preliminary, and neither the scope of the proposed transfer nor the employee movement has been finalised.

Bosch’s India Technology Footprint

Bosch established its Indian technology operations in Bengaluru in 1997 through Bosch Global Software Technologies (BGSW). Over the years, it expanded its presence to Hyderabad, Pune and Coimbatore.According to the report, India accounts for approximately four-fifths of Bosch’s global Global Capability Centre (GCC) workforce, which stands at around 28,900 employees.

Bengaluru accounts for approximately half of this workforce, while the remaining employees are based across the company's other Indian locations.The proposed transaction relates to Bosch's technology and product development operations and is separate from the business of listed Bosch Ltd, the Indian automotive components manufacturer.

Robert Bosch GmbH is the majority shareholder in Bosch Ltd through its promoter group companies. However, according to the report, Bosch Ltd does not directly oversee the GCC operations involved in the discussions.

TCS Expands Technology Capabilities

The potential transaction would add to TCS's recent acquisitions and strategic engagements involving captive technology and consulting operations. The IT services company has pursued such deals to strengthen its technology capabilities, expand its talent base and deepen relationships with global clients.In October, TCS acquired Best Buy's India technology centre. In August, it acquired Porsche's management and IT consulting arm, MHP, in a transaction valued at US$373 million. The company also secured a five-year IT modernisation contract with Porsche valued at US$1.45 billion.

The proposed Bosch transaction would follow a broader trend of multinational companies transferring captive technology centres to IT services providers. Such arrangements can provide service providers with access to established engineering teams and long-term service contracts, while allowing multinational companies to reassess their operating costs.

However, the transfer of employees from captive centres can also create initial margin pressures for acquiring IT services companies, particularly where existing salary structures are higher.Sushovon Nayak, Lead IT Analyst at Anand Rathi Institutional Equities, told Mint that long-term service contracts can help IT companies secure revenue over several years amid uncertain demand conditions.

Board Discussions To Determine Next Steps

The discussions between Bosch and TCS reflect the changing approach of multinational companies towards their captive technology operations, as IT services providers seek specialised engineering capabilities and more predictable revenue streams.The proposed transaction is still at an early stage, with board-level deliberations expected next month. The number of employees involved, the specific operations under consideration and the commercial terms remain uncertain.

If finalised, the deal could represent a significant movement of engineering talent from a multinational company's captive technology operations to an IT services provider in India's technology sector.

data.title: Karnataka Bank Names Udaya Kumar Hebbar MD And CEO
data.description:
The banking veteran takes on a three-year term, bringing experience across commercial banking, rural finance and microfinance

Karnataka Bank has appointed Udaya Kumar Hebbar as its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (MD and CEO) for a three-year term, following approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The approval was communicated through a letter dated 16 November 2026. The bank will inform the stock exchanges of the date on which Hebbar assumes charge.

Hebbar brings more than four decades of experience across banking, financial services, credit operations and rural finance. He previously served as Managing Director and CEO of CreditAccess Grameen from September 2010 to June 2025, leading the microfinance lender through a period of business expansion, an initial public offering (IPO) and subsequent capital raising.

Career Across Banking

Hebbar began his banking career at Corporation Bank in 1985, working across branch management, clearing and credit operations. He joined ICICI Bank in 1995, where his responsibilities included corporate credit, payment operations, centralised operations, quality initiatives, rural and micro banking, and agricultural business.

In 2007, he joined Barclays India as Head of Commercial and Payment Operations. His experience across banking operations, credit and rural financial services has shaped a career spanning traditional banking and financial inclusion.

Leadership At CreditAccess

Hebbar joined CreditAccess Grameen as Chief Executive Officer in 2010 and became its Managing Director and CEO in 2015. During his tenure, the company expanded its operations and customer base, with assets growing from Rs 250 cr in March 2011 to around Rs 26,000 cr by March 2025, according to his professional profile.

The lender also expanded its reach to more than 2,000 branches across 16 states and one Union Territory, serving over 4.8 million micro-borrowers as of March 2025. Hebbar led the company through its IPO in 2018 and a qualified institutional placement (QIP) in October 2020.

He retired from his executive role in June 2025 and continued as a Non-Executive Director on the company’s board.

Board And Leadership Roles

Hebbar currently holds non-executive positions across financial services and related organisations. These include Non-Executive Director roles at CreditAccess Grameen and CreditAccess Life Insurance, Non-Executive Chairman of CreditAccess India Foundation, and Deputy Chairperson of the Supervisory Board at CreditAccess India B.V.

A commerce graduate and postgraduate in commerce, Hebbar is also an Associate of the Indian Institute of Bankers (CAIIB). His leadership development includes programmes at Harvard Business School, INSEAD, IMD, London Business School and IESE.

Priorities At Karnataka Bank

Hebbar’s appointment brings experience in commercial banking, operational management and financial inclusion to Karnataka Bank’s leadership. His three-year term begins when he formally assumes charge, with the bank set to notify the stock exchanges of the effective date.

data.title: Cities Need More Than Buildings
data.description:
Dr Sanjeev Vidyarthi, Provost, Anant National University, on the need to rethink design education to address urbanisation, climate resilience and India's evolving cityscapes

India's rapid urbanisation and evolving environmental challenges call for a broader approach to design education, one that connects architecture with urban planning, technology, sustainability and social responsibility. In an email interaction with BW Education, Dr Sanjeev Vidyarthi, Provost, Anant National University, discusses the need for interdisciplinary curricula, industry-academia collaboration and responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) to prepare graduates for real-world challenges. Edited excerpts:

How can Indian design education move beyond conventional architecture training to address urbanisation, climate resilience and the complex challenges facing Indian cities?

Design and architecture education in India have notable strengths such as rigorous training and the impartation of a disciplined work ethic. However, translating imaginative studio work into practical solutions that address the complex challenges of rapid urbanisation, ongoing climate change and sustainable development remains an important task.

As India pursues the ideal of Viksit Bharat, architecture and design education needs to move beyond designing individual buildings and isolated institutional campuses towards a comprehensive understanding of cities, their communities and the relationship between people and their environment. This requires curricula integrating sustainability, technological innovations, contextual knowledge and interdisciplinary learning, while drawing upon India's regional diversity, traditional wisdom and Indigenous Knowledge Systems.

Understanding cities also requires recognising the interdependence of their physical infrastructure, natural environment, economic activities and social systems. Design interventions need to respond to these relationships rather than trying to address individual problems in isolation.

Ultimately, the objective is to prepare technologically adept and socially empathetic, responsible professionals with a broad understanding of complex situations they seek to address. Closer alignment between educational institutions, industry and policy frameworks will further strengthen their ability to shape built environments that are ecologically responsible, culturally responsive and economically resilient for the decades ahead.

What changes are needed in higher education curricula to bridge the gap between design theory, interdisciplinary learning and the practical demands of urban development?

Much of the India we envision for 2047 is currently being built and young professionals are already shaping the way India develops into Viksit Bharat. It is therefore essential to purposefully rethink and restructure higher education to nurture appropriately skilled professionals who can identify and address the diverse demands of our rapidly changing urban world.

To enable this change, higher education in India needs to break traditional disciplinary silos and take a more interdisciplinary pedagogical approach. HEIs must offer a more dynamic academic environment to students complemented by immersive learning experiences, community engagements, industry collaborations and regular opportunities to work on real-world problems.

They must also create stronger connections between classroom learning, studio work and professional practice. Students should have opportunities to test ideas, evaluate their feasibility and understand the practical constraints involved in implementation. Such an approach will help young professionals translate their knowledge into effective interventions.

Given your experience in establishing academic programmes in India and the US, what lessons can Indian universities draw from global models to strengthen design education while remaining rooted in local contexts?

Globally, design education has evolved via several pedagogical models, such as the Bauhaus, Ulm, Stanford d.school and Scandinavian approaches with globally lasting influences. These models offer important principles helpful to guide the development of the design discipline. While some emphasise the integration of art, craft and technology, others advance the understanding of design beyond aesthetics, establishing it as a rigorous, systematic discipline grounded in objective enquiry, empirical methods, iterative problem-solving and human-centred approaches, with a strong emphasis on social responsibility and long-term sustainability.

Many of these principles have shaped Indian design education. The opportunity now is to build upon these foundations through a diligent approach that combines the strengths of globally tried frameworks with a deeper understanding of India's diverse social fabric, rich cultural heritage and topical environmental concerns.

The use of clever design as a practical problem-solving tool is deeply ingrained in our cultural and social practices. Rather than simply replicating international models, Indian universities need to adapt their strengths to local conditions, drawing upon India's impressive regional and cultural diversity and century-old Indigenous Knowledge Systems. Such an approach will help develop educational models that are globally oriented but firmly grounded in Indian realities.

How can universities encourage research that connects architecture, urban planning, public policy and social equity, particularly in the context of India's rapidly expanding cities?

Teaching, research and practice are not separate domains but interconnected aspects of knowledge creation and communication. However, they are often perceived as distinct, leading to major gaps in delivery and educational experience. A strong academe-research-practice environment that brings together architects, urban planners, policymakers, social scientists and community stakeholders will enhance student learning and equip future professionals with relevant tools to carry out meaningful change in the world.

With artificial intelligence increasingly influencing architecture, urban planning and design, how should design institutions prepare students to use emerging technologies without compromising critical thinking, creativity and ethical judgement?

Emergent AI and other digital technologies are changing how products, services, buildings and infrastructure are conceived, designed, built, managed and evaluated. Yet, these technologies depend on human judgement, contextual understanding and interdisciplinary thinking to respond meaningfully to people, places and purpose.

These technologies, just like a sharp knife, can be put to socially good or totally disastrous ends, depending on how they are used - like a surgeon, chef or a criminal. Therefore, design institutions need to prepare students to harness AI and other similar technologies thoughtfully, as powerful tools that can improve the quality of life through clever thinking and better design.

Design education therefore needs to place informed emphasis on technological proficiency, critical thinking, creativity and ethical responsibility. The objective should be to prepare ethically sound professionals who can critically evaluate technological outputs, recognise their limitations and employ emerging technologies responsibly to develop socially beneficial solutions.

As provost of Anant National University, how do you assess whether design education is translating into meaningful career opportunities and enabling graduates to address real-world challenges beyond the classroom?

As the old adage goes, “The proof of the pudding is in the eating.” At Anant, we assess the contribution of our design education through the professional journeys of our graduates and their impact in the real world.

An encouraging indicator is the diversity of pathways our graduates pursue across manufacturing, advanced services, technology, education and the social sector. Our alumni are contributing to leading organisations such as Piramal Finance, Reliance, Accenture, Titan, TVS, Maruti, TCS and Teach For India, reflecting the relevance of design capabilities across domains.

Entrepreneurship is another significant outcome. Over the past three years alone, six of our graduates have established start-ups with annual turnovers of up to Rs 1 crore each, spanning healthcare, women's health and hygiene, robotics and sustainable manufacturing.

Ultimately, meaningful design education goes beyond conventional placement outcomes. It prepares appropriately skilled professionals to apply their knowledge across diverse contexts, create new opportunities and contribute meaningfully to society.

data.title: Alkem Laboratories gets USFDA warning letter with OAI classification for Daman facility
data.description:
Alkem Laboratories Ltd. on Thursday, November 19, said the US drug regulator has issued official action indicated (OAI) to the company's manufacturing facility in Amaliya, Daman.

The company said the US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) inspected the facility from April 20, 2026 to May 1, 2026 and issued the warning letter on November 18, 2026.

Alkem said the warning letter pertains to observations made by the USFDA during its inspection of the unit and requires the company to implement appropriate corrective and preventive actions to address the observations and prevent recurrence.

Alkem Labs said it will respond to the USFDA within the stipulated timeline. It added that it continues to manufacture and supply approved products from the facility to the US market.

The company added that there is no material impact on its current operation, financial or other activities of the company.

Alkem Laboratories reported its second quarter results earlier this month.

Its net profit declined 11.7% to ₹675.3 crore from ₹765 crore in the second quarter last year. Its revenue increased 13.8% to ₹4,552 crore from ₹4,001 crore last year.

The company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) increased 11.3% to ₹1,025 crore from ₹921 crore last year. Its EBITDA margin contracted by 50 basis points to 22.5% from 23% in the year-ago period.

Shares of Alkem Laboratories are trading 1.7% lower on Thursday at ₹5,133. The stock is down 6% so far this year.

data.title: Anandkumar Ramaraj Joins Barclays As Vice President – CFO Business Partner
data.description:
Ramaraj brings over 17 years of experience in business finance, financial planning and analysis, budgeting, forecasting and performance management

Barclays has appointed Anandkumar Ramaraj as Vice President – CFO Business Partner, according to an update shared by him on LinkedIn.

Ramaraj joins Barclays after working with Wells Fargo, where he served as Vice President – Business Finance Lead for Cards, Personal Loans, Retail Services and Auto Finance. He held the position from February 2026 to November 2026.

At Wells Fargo, he previously served as Senior AVP – Business Finance Lead for Cards, Merchant Services and Personal Loans from August 2024 to January 2026. Before that, he was Senior AVP – Finance Business Partner for Credit Cards from September 2022 to August 2024.

Ramaraj has over 17 years of experience in business finance and financial planning and analysis (FP&A). His professional experience includes business finance, budgeting, forecasting, performance management, financial modelling and business partnering.

Before joining Wells Fargo, he worked at Spice Money as Senior Manager from October 2021 to September 2022. He was associated with Jio Financial Services as Manager – Business Finance from March 2017 to October 2021, where he worked on zero-based budgeting for businesses including Payments Bank, payment gateway and insurance.

Earlier, he worked as Analyst III at BNY Mellon from August 2016 to March 2017.

Ramaraj holds an Executive Programme in Strategic Finance from the Indian Institute of Management, Lucknow, which he completed between February 2021 and January 2022. His LinkedIn profile also lists an association with Symbiosis Centre for Distance Learning.

data.title: JAKSON Green To Acquire Majority Stake In Ocior Energy
data.description:
The deal brings renewable energy, green hydrogen and ammonia capabilities under one platform, with projects spanning India and international markets

JAKSON Green has signed definitive agreements to acquire a majority stake in Ocior Energy India, in a move to expand its clean energy portfolio across renewable power and green fuels. The transaction will combine JAKSON Green’s capabilities in renewable energy, independent power production, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), and operations and maintenance (O&M) with Ocior Energy’s expertise in green hydrogen, green ammonia, green methanol and Power-to-X projects.

The companies expect the partnership to accelerate project development and strengthen their presence across the green molecules value chain. Financial details of the transaction, including the acquisition value and the precise stake to be acquired, were not disclosed in the announcement.

Expanding Clean Energy Portfolio

The acquisition will bring Ocior Energy’s green fuel projects into JAKSON Green’s broader clean energy platform. The combined capabilities are expected to support the development of projects across India, the Middle East and North Africa.

Green hydrogen and its derivatives, including green ammonia and green methanol, are emerging as potential alternatives to fossil fuels in sectors seeking to reduce emissions. The acquisition could help JAKSON Green expand beyond renewable power generation and project execution into the production and supply of these fuels.

Green Ammonia Projects

Ocior Energy’s portfolio includes 85,000 metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) of green ammonia supply awarded by the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) under an initial 10-year offtake agreement.

The company is also developing a green ammonia plant with a planned capacity of 200,000 MTPA in Gopalpur, Odisha. These projects add to its presence in the emerging green ammonia market, where long-term offtake arrangements can provide greater visibility on future demand.

Hydrogen Projects Under Development

Ocior Energy’s portfolio also includes two green hydrogen projects, each with a capacity of 5 kilotonnes per annum (KTPA). The projects are being developed for Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) in Madhya Pradesh and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) in Visakhapatnam.

The projects broaden the partnership’s exposure to green hydrogen production and industrial applications, alongside its ammonia development pipeline.

Global Expansion Plans

With a growing project pipeline across India, the Middle East and North Africa, the partnership aims to expand JAKSON Green’s international presence and accelerate the development of clean energy projects.

The acquisition’s eventual impact will depend on project execution, financing requirements, demand for green fuels and the ability to bring projects into commercial operation. The companies have not disclosed the transaction value or a completion timeline.

data.title: Cilicant Appoints Anil Acharya As Chief Financial Officer
data.description:
Acharya moves to Cilicant from Otis Elevator Company, where he most recently served as Regional Finance Head – West and Infrastructure Business

Cilicant has appointed Anil Acharya as its Chief Financial Officer (CFO), according to an announcement shared by the company on LinkedIn.

Acharya is a Chartered Accountant and Company Secretary with an MBA. He has experience in finance leadership across the manufacturing and industrial sectors.

Before joining Cilicant, Acharya was associated with Otis Elevator Company, where he most recently served as Regional Finance Head – West and Infrastructure Business. He held the position from December 2024 and was responsible for overseeing finance operations for a portfolio valued at $140 million, leading an 11-member team and reporting directly to the CFO.

He previously served as Regional Finance Head – West at Otis Elevator Company from February 2022 to November 2024. Before that, he held the position of Senior Manager – Finance between April 2019 and February 2022 and Manager – Finance from November 2016 to March 2019.

Earlier in his career, Acharya worked as Manager – Business Finance at Tata Motors from January 2015 to November 2016. He was also associated with KEC International as Assistant Manager – Finance and Accounts (FPNA) between August 2012 and January 2015.

His earlier professional experience includes working as Audit Manager at Khandelwal Jain & Co. from November 2010 to August 2012 and as an Auditor at Shambhu Gupta and Co. from September 2006 to October 2010.

Acharya completed his Chartered Accountancy qualification from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) between 2005 and 2010. He also holds a Company Secretary qualification from the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), which he pursued between 2007 and 2010.

In his professional profile, Acharya lists experience in accounts, financial controlling and taxation, along with financial procedures, budgeting, variance reporting, cost modelling, product costing and cost management.
